headline: Re-running a partially-failed inventory audit no longer double-applies its stock adjustments
summary: Finalizing an inventory audit with apply_adjustments writes one shelf adjustment per counted line through the stock-adjustment path, then marks the audit finalized. If a later line was refused mid-loop — most commonly a negative variance that would have pushed the shelf below its outstanding paid holds — the audit stayed open, but the lines already adjusted had moved their shelves. Re-running the finalize to clear the blocked line re-applied those earlier adjustments on top of themselves, debiting or crediting the same shelf twice. Finalize is now idempotent per line: before adjusting a shelf it checks whether this audit's adjustment for that SKU and location already landed, and skips it if so, so a retry only applies the lines that haven't been applied yet. The completing run reports the audit's full applied total. The final status flip is also gated on the audit still being open, so two finalizes racing the same audit can't both stamp it. No API change.

items.title: finalizeAudit is idempotent per line on retry
items.body: Each per-shelf adjustment is keyed by the audit's unique reason plus the line's SKU and location, which identify exactly one logical adjustment (an audit holds one line per SKU+location). Before adjusting a shelf, finalize checks whether that adjustment already exists and skips re-applying it. A finalize aborted partway — by a respect-holds floor refusal on a later line, or any transient failure — leaves the audit open and re-runnable; the retry applies only the lines that didn't land the first time, instead of double-counting the ones that did.

items.title: Audit finalization claims the open state
items.body: The transition that stamps an audit finalized now only lands while the audit is still open or in progress. Two finalize calls racing the same audit (or a duplicate retry that overlaps a completing run) collapse to a single finalization rather than re-stamping the completion time or overwriting the recorded variance totals.
